Q953.L1t: Blood components must be stored, handled and administered under strictly controlled conditions to keep recipients safe.
Q953.L2t: Red cell units are kept in a monitored blood bank fridge, and the time a unit may be out of controlled storage before transfusion is limited by local policy.
Q953.L3t: Once a unit has been out of controlled storage beyond the permitted time, its safety can no longer be guaranteed, so it must not be given or put back into general use, and the blood bank has to be told so that it can decide what happens to it and record it.
Q953.L4t: The unit should go back to the blood bank, with an explanation of why it is being returned.
Q953.L2f: Blood units must always be warmed to body temperature in a water bath before they are transfused, which is why they are taken out of the fridge early.
Q953.L3f: An out-of-time unit is classed as clinical waste that the ward is responsible for disposing of, and the empty bag is retained as the record of what happened.
Q953.L4f: The unit should be emptied in the sluice and the bag kept for records.

Q954.L1t: Urinary catheterization is an invasive procedure that is done with aseptic technique and attention to patient dignity and safety.
Q954.L2t: Before catheterizing, the nurse prepares the equipment, the environment and the patient, and checks that the sterile items are in date and intact.
Q954.L3t: Preparation covers things that affect the patient's own care and the safety of the procedure, such as agreement to treatment, hygiene and sterile equipment, and it does not include telling relatives, who have no part in the procedure itself.
Q954.L4t: Phoning the patient's next of kin is not a step that is done before catheterization.
Q954.L2f: Catheterization is a clean, non-sterile procedure, so equipment is not usually checked beforehand.
Q954.L3f: A competent adult's agreement is not needed for catheterization, because it is a routine nursing task covered by general admission consent.
Q954.L4f: Gaining the patient's consent is the step that is not done before catheterization.

Q916.L1t: Intravenous cannulae come in a range of sizes, and the gauge chosen depends on the patient and the reason for the infusion.
Q916.L2t: Gauge numbering is inverse, so a lower gauge number means a wider bore and a higher number means a finer needle.
Q916.L3t: A 14-16 gauge cannula is a very wide bore, which allows very fast flow of large volumes of fluid or blood, and this is needed when a patient is losing volume rapidly.
Q916.L4t: A 14-16 gauge needle is most likely to be used for trauma or burns patients.
Q916.L2f: Higher gauge numbers mean wider needles, so a 14-16 gauge needle is a fairly fine one.
Q916.L3f: Elderly patients have fragile, large and prominent veins that need the widest bore cannula to avoid collapse, so very low gauge numbers suit them best.
Q916.L4f: A 14-16 gauge needle is most likely to be used for elderly patients.
